lesson_title: Every Place Has a Seat Number
hook_text: Your exam asks for the exact position of a trig station. Here is how to give it an address precise to 31 metres.
clip_script: Every spot on earth has an address. Two numbers. Latitude, the rows, first. Longitude, the seats, second. South Africa is south of the equator and east of Greenwich, so every answer ends in S and E. A degree is chopped into 60 minutes, a minute into 60 seconds. One second is about 31 metres. On your map, the edges are ticked every minute. Join them, and the trig station sits in a box: 25 degrees 45 to 46 minutes south. Now the trap. Down south, numbers grow as you go down the map. So start at the top line. Measure down: 1,5 centimetres. The box is 3,7 centimetres. 1,5 over 3,7, times 60, is 24. 25 degrees 45 minutes 24 seconds south. Longitude: start at the left line, measure across, divide by the box width, times 60. 36 seconds. That trig station now has an address no one can mix up.
visual_style: A stadium ticket morphs into a globe with rows and seats; zoom into a map frame with minute ticks; pencil lines form a box; a ruler measures 1,5 of 3,7; numbers drop into a co-ordinate with S and E stamped at the end.
pacing: Snappy hook, quick globe review, slow on the trap, fast finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the seconds formula, working backwards from co-ordinates and quick estimate checks.
